summary.text: Writing $X=2^{2^{33}}$, if $F_{33}=X+1$ is prime then $\varphi(m)\ge X$ and $\varphi(m)<m$ force every admissible $m$ to satisfy $m\ge F_{33}$, while $\varphi(F_{33})=X$. If $F_{33}$ is composite, any hypothetical $m<2X$ must have $\varphi(m)=X$; writing $m=2^k r$ with $r$ odd, the cases $k\le1$ would make $r$ a squarefree product of Fermat primes $F_i$ with $i\le33$, and excluding $F_{33}$ gives $r\le\prod_{i<33}F_i=F_{33}-2<X<r$, while for $k\ge2$ multiplicativity of the totient and $\varphi(r)<r$ force $m\ge2X$ (with equality when $r=1$).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad X=2^N=2^{2^{33}},\qquad F_i=2^{2^i}+1,
\]
so in particular
\[
F_{33}=X+1.
\]
For a nonnegative integer \(n\), let
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

We first collect the number-theoretic facts needed for the lower bounds.

For every positive integer \(m\), Euler's totient satisfies
\[
0<\varphi(m)\le m,
\]
and if \(m>1\), then in fact \(\varphi(m)<m\). Also, if \(d\mid m\), then
\[
\varphi(d)\mid\varphi(m).
\]
The latter follows directly from the prime-power formula
\(\varphi(p^j)=p^{j-1}(p-1)\): if \(d\mid m\), each prime occurs in \(d\) to no larger an exponent than in \(m\), and the corresponding prime-power totient divides the one for \(m\). We will also use multiplicativity of the totient on coprime factors and, in particular,
\[
\varphi(2^k)=2^{k-1}\quad(k\ge 1).
\]

We need a structural result about odd integers with power-of-two totient.

**Lemma 1.** Suppose \(m\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(m)=2^K.
\]
Then:

1. \(m\) is squarefree;
2. every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) is a Fermat number \(F_i\) which is prime;
3. for such a divisor \(p=F_i\), one has \(2^i\le K\).

To prove this, let \(p\mid m\) be prime. Since \(\varphi(p)=p-1\) divides \(\varphi(m)=2^K\), every divisor of \(p-1\) is a power of two, and hence
\[
p-1=2^e
\]
for some \(e\le K\). Because \(m\) is odd, \(p\ne2\), so \(e>0\).

We now use the standard characterization of primes of the form \(2^e+1\). Write
\[
e=2^i q
\]
with \(q\) odd. If \(q>1\), put \(y=2^{2^i}\). Then
\[
2^e+1=y^q+1
\]
is divisible by \(y+1\), because \(q\) is odd; both factors are nontrivial. This contradicts the primality of \(p=2^e+1\). Therefore \(q=1\), so \(e=2^i\), and
\[
p=2^{2^i}+1=F_i.
\]
Since \(e\le K\), this also gives \(2^i\le K\).

It remains to prove squarefreeness. If \(p^2\mid m\) for some prime \(p\), then
\[
\varphi(p^2)=p(p-1)\mid\varphi(m)=2^K.
\]
In particular, \(p\mid2^K\), so the prime \(p\) must be \(2\). But \(m\) is odd, so \(2\nmid m\), a contradiction. Thus no prime square divides \(m\), proving the lemma.

We next specialize this structure to the exponent \(N=2^{33}\).

**Lemma 2.** If \(m\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(m)=X=2^{2^{33}},
\]
then \(F_{33}\) is prime.

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. By Lemma 1, every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) has the form \(F_i\), and its index satisfies
\[
2^i\le 2^{33}.
\]
Since powers of \(2\) are strictly increasing, this means \(i\le33\). The case \(i=33\) is impossible: it would say that the prime \(p\) equals the nonprime number \(F_{33}\). Hence every prime divisor of \(m\) is among
\[
F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_{32}.
\]
Moreover, Lemma 1 says that \(m\) is squarefree. Consequently \(m\) is the product of some subset of these numbers, and therefore
\[
m\le\prod_{i=0}^{32}F_i.
\]
Here each omitted factor is greater than \(1\), so adjoining all the factors can only increase the product.

The Fermat numbers satisfy the product identity
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}F_i=F_r-2=2^{2^r}-1.
\]
For completeness, this follows by induction. For \(r=0\), the empty product is \(1=F_0-2\). If the identity holds for \(r\), then, writing \(z=2^{2^r}\),
\[
\left(\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}F_i\right)F_r=(z-1)(z+1)=z^2-1
=2^{2^{r+1}}-1=F_{r+1}-2.
\]
Taking \(r=33\), we obtain
\[
m\le F_{33}-2=X-1<X.
\]
On the other hand, \(X>1\), and \(\varphi(m)=X\le m\) implies \(m>1\). Hence the strict totient inequality gives
\[
X=\varphi(m)<m,
\]
contradicting \(m<X\). This contradiction proves Lemma 2.

We now prove the two cases of the claimed formula.

### Case 1: \(F_{33}\) is prime

First, \(F_{33}\) itself is admissible. Indeed,
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=X=2^N,
\]
so \(2^N\mid\varphi(F_{33})\).

We show that no smaller positive integer is admissible. Let \(m>0\) satisfy
\[
X=2^N\mid\varphi(m).
\]
Since \(\varphi(m)>0\), divisibility implies
\[
X\le\varphi(m)\le m.
\]
Because \(X>1\), this shows \(m>1\), and hence \(\varphi(m)<m\). Therefore
\[
X\le\varphi(m)<m,
\]
so, as these are integers,
\[
F_{33}=X+1\le m.
\]
Thus every admissible \(m\) is at least \(F_{33}\), while \(F_{33}\) is itself admissible. Consequently
\[
a(N)=F_{33}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is prime.

### Case 2: \(F_{33}\) is not prime

Set
\[
B=2^{N+1}=2X.
\]
This number is admissible because
\[
\varphi(B)=\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N=X.
\]
It remains to prove that every admissible positive integer \(m\) satisfies \(m\ge B\).

Suppose for contradiction that
\[
0<m<B
\quad\text{and}\quad
X\mid\varphi(m).
\]
Since \(\varphi(m)>0\), there is a positive integer \(c\) such that
\[
\varphi(m)=cX.
\]
But
\[
\varphi(m)\le m<B=2X,
\]
so \(0<c<2\), forcing \(c=1\). Hence
\[
\varphi(m)=X. \tag{1}
\]

Write the unique decomposition of \(m\) into its power-of-two and odd parts as
\[
m=2^k r,
\]
where \(k\ge0\) and \(r\) is odd. We divide into cases according to \(k\).

If \(k=0\), then \(m=r\) is odd. Equation (1) and Lemma 2 imply that \(F_{33}\) is prime, contrary to the assumption of this case.

If \(k=1\), then \(m=2r\), with \(r\) odd. Since \(2\) and \(r\) are coprime and \(\varphi(2)=1\), multiplicativity gives
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(2)\varphi(r)=\varphi(r).
\]
Thus (1) says \(\varphi(r)=X\). Again \(r\) is odd, so Lemma 2 would imply that \(F_{33}\) is prime, another contradiction.

It remains to consider \(k\ge2\). Since \(r\) is odd, \(2^k\) and \(r\) are coprime. Therefore (1) and multiplicativity give
\[
2^{k-1}\varphi(r)=\varphi(2^k)\varphi(r)=\varphi(m)=2^N. \tag{2}
\]

First suppose \(r=1\). Equation (2) becomes
\[
2^{k-1}=2^N,
\]
so \(k-1=N\), hence \(k=N+1\). It follows that
\[
m=2^k=2^{N+1}=B,
\]
contrary to the assumption \(m<B\).

Finally suppose \(r\ne1\). As \(r\) is a positive odd integer, this implies \(r\ge3\), and therefore
\[
\varphi(r)<r. \tag{3}
\]
Equation (2) shows that \(2^{k-1}\mid2^N\), hence \(k-1\le N\), and cancellation of \(2^{k-1}\) in (2) yields
\[
\varphi(r)=2^{N-(k-1)}. \tag{4}
\]
Using (3) and (4), we obtain the strict estimate
\[
\begin{aligned}
m=2^k r
&>2^k\varphi(r)\\
&=2^k\,2^{N-(k-1)}\\
&=2^{k+N-(k-1)}\\
&=2^{N+1}=B.
\end{aligned}
\]
This again contradicts \(m<B\).

Every possible value of \(k\) has led to a contradiction. Thus no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(B=2^{N+1}\). Since \(B\) itself is admissible, it is the minimum, and
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is not prime.

Combining the two cases and recalling \(N=2^{33}\), we conclude
\[
\boxed{
 a(2^{33})=
 \begin{cases}
 2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
 2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}}
\]
